about: The golden fixture for the pdc1 device credential: every way a leaf can fail to
be somebody, as inputs plus the verdict every Peachy client must reach.
The sibling of rules.json - that one pins what the GROUP policy decides, this one
pins what the IDENTITY layer decides, and the two are the whole of what four
clients have to agree on before any of them ships.
docs/mls-core.md 'Golden credential fixture' is the reading guide,
mls/core/src/identity.rs and mls/core/src/credential.rs are the checks, and
mls/core/src/fixture.rs is the door a replay calls.
Written in NAMES, never numbers, for the same reason as rules.json: a reader has
to be able to read a row and say whether it is what Peachy means. The numbers ride
along in reasonCode so that a rename which left the discriminant alone, and a
renumbering which left the name alone, both fail here.
KEY MATERIAL IS SYNTHESISED, NEVER REAL. Every key in this file is a 32-byte seed
written out as 64 hex characters, chosen to be recognisable rather than random:
0707..07  the Peachy server's current signing key   (kid fe812c12)
0808..08  the server key from before a rotation     (kid 5c29b78f)
0909..09  an impostor's key, trusted by nobody      (kid dbc29825)
1111..11  Ada's device key
2222..22  an attacker's device key
3333..33  Bo's device key
a1a1..a1  Ada's ACCOUNT key (the account store's secret); her account identity
key, which signs for each of her devices, is derived from it
a2a2..a2  another account's key
Nothing here is, or could be mistaken for, a key any Peachy environment holds; the
real one is held only by the server, and exactly one process mints credentials
with it.
ONE KEY, ONE FORMAT. A trust entry written as a bare seed publishes that
issuer's key the way a live /healthz/device-credential-keys does, as a device
key. An entry written as { seed, use } publishes it under that use instead, and
a verifier trusts only device-use keys: any other use is dropped, never guessed
at.
TIME IS PINNED. nowUnix is 1789516800 - 2026-09-16T00:00:00Z, a fixed instant,
and the same one mls/core/tests/support uses.
An expiry case written against the wall clock is a case that starts failing on a
date nobody chose, so every case says what the verifier's clock reads.
Each case carries its own inputs WHOLE: no defaults are merged in from this
top level, because a merge would be a second opinion about the fixture's shape,
held once more in every binding. The case object goes to the door verbatim.
Replayed by every client, each through its own door and none of them
re-deciding anything: mls/core/tests/credentials_fixture.rs (Rust),
mls/wasm/tests/node/credentials.test.mjs (JavaScript, through the wasm binding),
mls/swift/Tests/PeachyMLSTests/CredentialsFixtureTests.swift and
the Android binding's `CredentialsFixtureTest` (not in this repository) (the last two
through peachy_mls_fixture_evaluate_case in the C ABI - the same single entry
point rules.json goes through, which is why a case names its kind).
All TWELVE live CredentialRejection codes are reached by some case, and every replay
asserts that. A rejection nothing produces is a branch this fixture cannot
protect, and it could go wrong in one client with nothing anywhere going red.
The five 'order/' cases are the other half: a verifier that answers the right
set of questions in the wrong ORDER still tells a person the wrong thing about
why their device was refused, and every one of those orderings is deliberate.
THE ACCOUNT CERTIFICATE (docs/identity.md 'The account identity key'). A
mint with accountKey carries Ada's account identity key and its signature over the
device key; without one both fields are empty, which is a device its account has
not let in. validateMember is the door a PEER's leaf comes through - a key package
being added, a leaf in a tree - and it refuses such a device as not_approved; the
other two doors are the device's own, and accept it so a waiting device can open.
validateOwn is the device's own credential checked against the account key it holds
(heldAccountKey): a certificate under any other identity key is not_own_account_key,
a device holding no account key opens only uncertified (any certificate is
not_own_account_key: it names a key the device cannot check), and no certificate
at all still opens.

codes.note: The pinned #[repr(u32)] discriminants of CredentialRejection. A replay does not need these - it compares names and reasonCode - but a reader of a Swift or Kotlin port does, and mls/core/src/error.rs has a unit test asserting the same numbers. The first five mirror VerifyFailure in the server's credential issuer one for one; the rest are checks only a LEAF verifier can make (implausible_lifetime bounds a group's tree clock, which means nothing to the server that issued the token), and not_own_account_key one only the device itself can make, against the account key it holds. 9 (wrong_key_use) is retired and never reused.

seeds.note: Repeated here only so a reader can match a case's hex to a name. The door reads the hex out of each case and never looks at this block.

cases.why: The ordinary case, and the only one that proves the others are about something. An acceptance carries the whole KEY layer back - actor, device, which server key vouched, when it runs out - because a verdict that said only 'accepted' would read the same from a verifier that had stopped looking at the payload at all.

Issued 30 seconds in this verifier's future. Clocks disagree, and a credential minted moments ago by a slightly fast server is not a forgery - CLOCK_SKEW_SECONDS is 60, matching what the server allows itself.

iat is now + 60 exactly. The comparison is `now + skew < iat`, so the boundary is INSIDE the allowance - paired with not_yet_valid/one-second-beyond-the-skew, which is the same case one second later. An off-by-one here would pass both of those in isolation and only one of them together.
The other boundary. `exp` is exclusive - now >= exp is expired - so one second before it is still good, and expired/exactly-at-exp is the same credential one second on.

The verifier holds two server keys, as GET /healthz/device-credential-keys serves them after a rotation (the retired keys it still publishes, docs/identity.md). A credential minted before the rotation keeps checking out for its whole lifetime, which is the entire point of publishing the previous key at all - and the verdict names the OLD kid, so a verifier that quietly re-attributed it to the current key fails here.

The same token, reached the way a leaf reaches it: wrapped in a BasicCredential rather than handed over bare. Peachy ships pdc1 inside credential type 0x0001 rather than registering a type of its own (mls/core/src/credential.rs), so this is the path every real leaf takes and it must answer identically to validateToken.
No bytes at all. A leaf with an empty credential is not a leaf with a bad credential, but it is refused before anything else can be asked about it.
The prefix and nothing else. A pdc1 token is exactly three dot-separated parts.

Any prefix but pdc1 is not a credential. The prefix is refused at the shape check, before the payload's own `v` is ever looked at - which is why unsupported_version needs a pdc1 token to reach it. malformed/a-signed-person-payload-under-another-prefix is the same refusal over a token that is otherwise perfect.
Three parts and no more. A fourth segment is where an extension would smuggle itself in, and there is no extension.
Right shape, unreadable segments.

Valid base64url in both segments, but the signature decodes to five bytes. The length is checked before Ed25519 is asked anything, so this is malformed and not a bad signature - the difference matters to whoever reads the log.

A signature segment of the right LENGTH (86 base64url characters, 64 bytes of zeroes) over a payload segment that decodes to the five letters of 'hello'. This is the one that reaches the JSON parse, which nothing above it does.
A well-signed payload naming no server key. Empty is not 'unknown': there is nothing to look up, so it never reaches the trust set.

A credential that binds a device to nobody. actor_id is the KEY layer of identity (docs/identity.md); an empty one would produce a PeachyIdentity that identifies nothing, which is worse than a refusal.
The same, for the device half. A credential names one actor AND one device; either missing and the binding says nothing.

An id is 1-64 bytes of [A-Za-z0-9._-]. A newline is the separator a list of ids was once joined with, so an id holding one could pass for two devices, or hide one behind another; it is refused at parse, before anything reads the id.
The same charset rule for '#', which the new-device notice uses to write a device id beside a key it was not first seen holding (<id>#<64 hex>). An id holding one could pass for that form.
The charset rule holds for the actor id too: a person's id is never two people's.
An id is at most 64 bytes: a server-chosen id is a UUID, 36 bytes, and nothing longer is ever a name for one device.

The payload's device_key is standard base64 of a raw Ed25519 key, and this is not base64 at all. Refused at the shape check, so no comparison with the leaf is ever attempted - a verifier that reached leaf_key_mismatch here would be comparing against bytes it had invented.

Valid base64 of three bytes. An Ed25519 public key is exactly 32, and a short one that got as far as the leaf comparison would answer leaf_key_mismatch - a wrong and confusing thing to tell somebody whose credential is simply corrupt.

MAX_TOKEN_BYTES is 8 KiB - a bound on the work a malformed leaf can cause, sized well above a post-quantum payload and deliberately not a format rule. 9,000 characters of actor id carry the token past it, and it is refused before any signature is verified. actorIdFill exists so this case can be written without burying the forty characters that matter under nine thousand that do not.

Signed by a key this verifier DOES hold, but the payload names a different one. The kid is a lookup hint and not a security claim, so the answer is about the lookup: nothing to check the signature against.

A perfectly good credential against a client that has never fetched GET /healthz/device-credential-keys. Every leaf is then an unknown kid, which is the honest answer and reads as 'fetch the key list', not as 'this person is a forger'.

The sharpest forgery available: take the trusted kid - eight public, guessable hex characters - and sign with your own key. It is the case that makes the difference between unknown_kid and bad_signature load-bearing, because an implementation that merely checked 'is this kid known' would accept it.

A genuine credential whose payload segment has been swapped for a well-formed payload naming a different actor, over the original signature. This is the forgery that works against a verifier which re-serializes what it parsed instead of checking the bytes as they ARRIVED - the one rule mls/core/src/credential.rs states in its header and the one this case exists to hold.

One character of the signature segment changed. The length still checks out, so this reaches Ed25519 rather than stopping at the shape check - which is what separates it from malformed/signature-is-not-64-bytes.

Expired, and named as such rather than folded into a general invalidity: a person whose device credential has run out needs to be told to renew it, which is a different sentence from every other rejection here.

now == exp. The boundary is EXCLUSIVE on both sides of the wire, the same way the server's credential issuer reads it; paired with accept/one-second-before-expiry, which is this credential one second earlier.
Ten hours of head start is not a clock disagreement. Its own name because the operational answer differs: expired means renew, not-yet-valid means one of the two clocks is wrong.
iat is now + 61, one second past the 60 the verifier allows. The pair to accept/exactly-at-the-skew-boundary: together they pin the boundary, and neither of them alone does.

Issued at yesterday's UTC midnight and expiring thirty-one days later, to the second: the longest credential the issuer gives (the server's credential issuer floors iat to a UTC midnight and rounds exp UP to the midnight at or after issue + thirty days). MAX_CREDENTIAL_LIFETIME_SECONDS is an inclusive bound, and this is the pair to implausible_lifetime/one-second-longer-than-thirty-one-days.

The same credential one second longer, signed by the real key: live, bound to the right leaf, and still refused. A credential that may claim any lifetime may claim an iat years ahead with an exp to match, and iat is what a group's tree clock is made of - one such leaf pushed every other leaf past its grace on that clock and froze the group's membership for good (docs/identity.md 'A received commit is judged on the tree clock'). An OLD credential still answers expired before it answers this: expired/one-second-past is forty days long and must stay expired.

iat is now + 60 (inside the skew, so not not_yet_valid) and exp is now + 30 (not yet passed, so not expired): a credential that expires before it was issued. No issuer means that, and a verifier that only compared each end to its own clock would accept it.

Ada's credential is a PUBLIC artefact - anyone who has seen one of her messages has seen it. Replayed onto a leaf signing with an attacker's key it must buy nothing, and this is the only check that says so. It is the line that gives the whole credential its meaning: an attacker cannot make their leaf sign with Ada's device key.

The same replay, wrapped in the BasicCredential a real leaf carries. validateCredential and validateToken must not drift apart on the one check that makes a leaf mean anything, and the only way to say so is to ask both.

A pdc1-prefixed token whose payload says v: 2. A future format must fail LOUDLY on an old client rather than be read with today's rules - the failure mode a version field exists to prevent, and one that only shows up years later if it is got wrong.

RFC 9420's other standard credential type. Peachy leaves carry exactly one shape, and an X.509 chain - however valid - is not it. Note the token inside is a GOOD pdc1 credential: the refusal is about the envelope, and a verifier that unwrapped first would accept it.

A type from the registry that this build has never heard of. 'Anything that is not basic' has to be one branch and not a list of the types a reader happened to think of, or the first new registration is an accepted leaf nobody checked.

GREASE exists precisely to catch implementations that special-case the types they know (RFC 9420 section 13.5). A GREASE credential arriving at a Peachy leaf is refused like any other unknown type, rather than crashing or being read as basic.

A forgery under a trusted kid that is ALSO long expired. The answer is bad_signature, because nothing the payload says - including its dates - means anything until the signature says the payload is the server's. A verifier that checked the clock first would tell a forger 'renew your credential'.

Signed by the impostor under the impostor's own kid. Both 'we do not hold that key' and 'that signature is not ours' are true; the first is what gets said, because it is the one an operator can act on - after a rotation it means 'refresh the key list'.

Expired AND replayed onto the wrong leaf. Expired wins, because the clock is checked before the binding - and that ordering is the kindest one: the overwhelmingly common reason a real leaf fails is that its credential ran out, and telling that person their key does not match would send them looking for an attacker.

A pdc1 token whose payload claims v: 2, under a kid nobody holds. The version is part of the SHAPE and is read during parsing, before the trust set is consulted at all - so a client meeting a version it does not know is told the truth about why, rather than being sent to refetch a key list that would not help.

An X.509 credential whose contents are not a token at all. The type is refused first, so the bytes inside are never parsed - which is the point of checking the envelope: an unknown credential type is not an invitation to go looking for something readable inside it.

A verifier reads only device-use keys off the published list and drops every other use rather than guess at it, so a list holding the right seed under any other use trusts nothing, and an ordinary pdc1 under it is an unknown kid - fetch the list again - rather than a person.

An ordinary v: 1 payload that would verify under pdc1, signed by the trusted key, under any other prefix. Refused: the prefix is the format, and the only format is pdc1, so a validly signed token in some other format is never read as a person.

The smuggle: a v: 1 pdc1, signed by the trusted key, with a field beside its own that this format does not have. A verifier that skipped unknown fields would read this as Ada's device and drop the field on the floor; every client refuses the whole token instead.

The ordinary case since the account identity key (docs/identity.md 'The account identity key'). Ada's laptop carries her account's signature over its device key, checked at the peer's door, and the verdict names the account key so the reader can compare it with the key it pinned for Ada. a1a1..a1 is Ada's ACCOUNT key (the account store's secret); the identity key is derived from it.
The same credential through the door a device's OWN client opens on. Accepted, with the account key.
A device nobody on the account has let in yet: both account fields empty. Its own client still opens on it, because a device waiting for approval has to hold a credential to be approved at all.

The same credential at the door a PEER's leaf comes through. Refused as not_approved: the server vouched for the device and no device of Ada's did, so it is not added to anything and no message is encrypted to it. This is the server-added device, and it is refused in silence.

Ada's real account identity key in the payload, beside a signature made by a different account's key. The forgery a server can attempt: copy the public key everyone has seen and sign with one it holds. Refused as account_signature, whichever door it comes through.
An account key with the signature left empty. Both fields or neither: half a certificate is malformed, never a device that is half let in.
An expired credential that also carries a bad account signature answers expired: the account check comes last, after everything the server's own signature covers.
This device's own credential, certified under the identity key derived from the account key it holds. It opens, and the key it carries is that one.

The server answered this device's registration with a credential certified under an account key of its own: well signed by the server, with an account signature that verifies under the key it names. Only the device holding the real account key can tell, and it refuses to run on it as not_own_account_key. Taken as its own, that key would let a device the server made share this person's seat and make both halves of a security code agree.

No certificate at all, at a device that holds an account key: what a device holding a stale key registers with while it waits to be let in. It names no key that could be another's, so its own client opens.

A device still waiting to be let in holds no account key, and the server answered its registration with a credential certified under a key of its own. A certificate is something a device can make only once it holds the key, so it has nothing to check this one against and refuses it as not_own_account_key; it runs uncertified until it holds the key. Taken as given, the device would run on the server's key after it was approved, and the groups it joined meanwhile would keep it there.

Ada's approved laptop, signed by the trusted key, with one space after the payload's opening brace. A credential is read only in its one canonical spelling, so that its length is a function of its fields: were any spelling read, the issuer could give each device a token of its own length and read the device off the growth of every renewal and leaf rotation it makes. Without the space this is account/an-approved-device-on-its-own, accepted.

The same credential with both base64url segments written with '=' padding. The decoded bytes and the signature are unchanged, so only the canonical-spelling rule refuses it, for the same reason: a longer spelling of the same token is a length the issuer chose.

device_key is Ada's real key in standard base64 without its '=' padding, signed by the trusted key. The canonical spelling of a key field is padded, as the server writes it, so a key that decodes to the right 32 bytes in another spelling is still malformed.

The trusted key's kid in capitals, signed by that key. A kid is the first eight hex characters of SHA-256 over the server's public key, in lowercase, and nothing else: a kid of any other shape or length is malformed before the trust set is consulted, so it cannot carry a length of the issuer's choosing either.

An application message's sender, judged as every receiver judges it (docs/identity.md 'A revoked leaf's messages'): the credential checks as a member's does, without the expiry, and then the message. receivedAt is the second the delivery service received it. A live credential the reader holds no revocation for is read.
Ada's laptop lapsed a day ago on the reader's wall, and the message was received before that: read, inside the grace, and marked lapsed.
Past exp plus the 56-day grace on the reader's wall, nothing from the leaf is read, whenever it was received.

The reader holds a revocation of the laptop's device key signed by Ada's own account key, which the delivery service said took effect at revokedAt, and the message was received after it. Refused, live credential or not. The verdict names no credential rejection: the credential is sound, and it is its account that signed the key out.
The same revocation, and a message the delivery service received before it took effect: sent while the laptop was still Ada's, so it is read, however late the reader reads it.
Received in the very second the revocation took effect: not before it, so refused.
No receivedAt: the reader cannot place the message before the revocation, and an unknown time counts as after. Refused.
No revokedAt: the revocation came without the time it took effect, so nothing can be placed before it. Refused, however early the message was received.
A revocation of the laptop's key signed by some other account (a2a2..a2) does not verify under the account key Ada's credential names, and is no revocation: the message is read.

Ada's laptop lapsed a day ago, and the delivery service received the message after that: a lapsed leaf's NEW message, whatever epoch it was sealed in (docs/identity.md 'A lapsed leaf's new messages'). Refused as expired.

Received, says the delivery service, before Ada's laptop lapsed, but sealed in the reader's current epoch, whose tree clock (treeClock, a member's signed iat) is past her exp: a date the sender cannot move says it is new, and it is refused as expired.
Received before Ada's laptop lapsed, and sealed in an epoch whose tree clock is before her exp: history, read inside the grace and marked lapsed only.
No receivedAt, and the reader's wall is past Ada's exp: nothing places the message before it, so it counts as new and is refused as expired.
A live credential, sealed in the reader's current epoch: a tree clock before exp changes nothing.
